msItem.incipit: Here lies his frailty his fair soul above Folger First Line Index

abstract.p: The poem is an epitaph that commemorates Mr Inglethorpp by contrasting the frailty of his body with the enduring worth of his soul. It presents his life as purposefully directed toward virtuous ends, emphasizing his civic reputation, generosity, and hospitality, and portraying him as both “the city’s glory” and a perpetual friend to the poor. While invoking classical comparison through Jove, the speaker ultimately rejects the adequacy of praise, suggesting that his virtue exceeds the capacity of language to represent it. The closing couplet resolves this by reducing commemoration to the simple act of inscription, where naming the deceased is itself sufficient testimony to his merit.

lg.l: Heere lies his frailty his faier soule above,
Who sorted all His actions to that end:
This Cytties Glory everie goods mans Love,
In life in death the poores perpetuall Freind:
As Hospitable as they speake of Jove.
And o his zeale! But how dare wee Commend?
Beyonde all penns his praise will best appeare,
Only to write tis Inglethorpp lies heere.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: Richard Inglethorpe (1560–1619) was a Worcester clothier, merchant, and civic official, serving as City Chamberlain in 1602 and High Bailiff in 1610. Having amassed considerable wealth through trade and extensive property holdings, he died without children and, by his will of 4 July 1618 (NA PROB_11_133_624), directed that his estate be used for charitable purposes. His endowment funded almshouses, established c. 1620, for six aged or infirm poor men of the city and a woman to attend them, supported by income from his properties. The poem edited here is the same as the text of his memorial inscription in Worcester Cathedral.
